bga_name: In The Year of the Dragon
rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Round Order 1.1 1st Phase: Choose an Action 1.2 2nd Phase: Choose a New Person 1.3 3rd Phase: Event 1.4 4th Phase: Scoring 2 Events 2.1 Peace 2.2 Imperial Tribute 2.3 Drought 2.4 Mongol Invasion 2.5 Dragon Festival 2.6 Epidemic 3 Actions 3.1 Taxes 3.2 Build 3.3 Harvest 3.4 Fireworks Display 3.5 Military Parade 3.6 Research 3.7 Privilege 3.8 (No action) 4 End-of-game Scoring 4.1 Person 4.2 Monk 4.3 Rice and Fireworks Round Order The game consists of exactly 12 rounds, symbolising the 12 months in the Year of the Dragon. The player order for the round is determined by the marker positions of the Persons track. Each round consists of the following 4 phases, in order: 1st Phase: Choose an Action If you choose an action in the same grouping as another player has already chosen, you must pay 3 yuan. You may also choose no action and fill your personal money supply to 3 yuan. 2nd Phase: Choose a New Person If you do not have available space in any palaces, you must discard a different person before placing your new person. You need a card with the given role of the person you want to take or the wild card Gain positions on the Persons track a number of spaces equal to the value of the new person you selected. 3rd Phase: Event After the event resolves, any palaces which are unoccupied lose 1 floor. 4th Phase: Scoring 1 point for each: Palace Court lady Privilege (small) 2 points for large privilege Events Peace Nothing happens Imperial Tribute Each player pays 4 yuan For each yuan a player is short, release 1 person Drought Each player must turn in 1 rice tile for each inhabited palace From each unsupplied palace, release 1 person Mongol Invasion Each player scores points equal to the helmets on their warriors All the players with the fewest must each release a single person Dragon Festival Players get 6, or 3, victory points for the most, or the second most, fireworks Scoring players then turn in half of their tiles to the supply Epidemic Each player must release 3 persons, 1 fewer per mortar on their healers Actions Taxes Take 1 yuan from the supply for each coin symbol (on the action card and the player’s tax collectors ) Build Take 1 palace floor from the supply for each hammer (on the action card and the player’s craftsmen ), then build the new floors; no palace higher than 3 floors Harvest Take 1 rice tile from the supply for each rice sack (on the action card and the player’s farmers ) Fireworks Display Take 1 fireworks tile from the supply for each rocket (on the action card and the player’s pyrotechnists ) Military Parade Move 1 space on the person track for each helmet (on the card and the player’s warriors ) Research Move 1 space on the scoring track for each book (on the action card and the player’s scholars ) Privilege Pay 2, or 6 (or 7 depending on new or old edition rules), yuan to the supply and take a small, or large, privilege tile from the supply accordingly (No action) Take up to 3 yuan from the supply to bring your total yuan to 3 End-of-game Scoring Person 2 points each Monk [ number of Buddhas ] x [ number of floors ] points Rice and Fireworks Each player sells back to the supply all of their rice and fireworks tiles for 2 yuan each. Afterwards, each player earns 1 victory point for every 3 yuan they possess.

community_text:
[Rating: 3/10] People always say that The Castles of Burgundy is the blandest looking game they've seen. They clearly haven't seen this one.

[Rating: 5/10] I really wish the game just focused on the managing a bad year part and avoided giving you the dragon/emperor's favour tokens. Dealing with a bunch of events and doing it rather badly almost feels like some kind of subtle swipe at government administration. I really wish the the rest of the game ran wild with that concept.

[Rating: 5/10] What an annoyingly dated game. Some good things in it, but needs more to age well today. Probably the worst Feld I have played!

[Rating: 5/10] First impression: Eh. Quite dry and procedural. No big moments or surprises. It’s a decent puzzle and a solid game that plays fast at 5, but I was ready for it to be over by month 10 or so.

[Rating: 5/10] This game rubbed me the wrong way for some reason. Props to it for modeling how miserable Chinese history was for most Chinese people. :(

[Rating: 5/10] This is a very strange game. There's no avoiding bad events: you can only minimize their effects. That's the game: trying to maximize your points while experiencing all those negatives. You will lose people, so make sure you use them before you lose them and score points when you can.  Even though I know that's the game, I don't quite get it. I find the very limited engine building, which is more lateral than forward, deeply unsatisfying. [Rating: 5/10] Not in love but don't hate it. It's an alright short tile game. Players could be huge dicks if they wanted to while playing with you.   Player Count: 2-5

[Rating: 5/10] Across multiple rounds players are managing their tableau, by building up their buildings, gaining more people (which can gain points/military/food/etc), and managing events that deter players. Players will place a worker gaining resources/points, then using one of their meeple to gain a person into their buildings, and then resolving events. Player with the most points wins.
